articles.title: Middleton's Regeneration Accelerates with Key Developments Announced
articles.excerpt: Middleton's regeneration initiative has gained momentum with three significant announcements, including plans for the historic Middleton Old Grammar School and the repurposing of the Scout Hut for community use.
articles.content_html:
Middleton's regeneration initiative has taken a significant step forward with three key announcements made during an event at Middleton Arena on 16 September 2026. The event, attended by over 500 residents and local business leaders, was chaired by the proposed chairs of Middleton's Mayoral Development Corporation, Steve Coogan and Rose Marley, alongside Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig and Rochdale Borough Council leader, Councillor Neil Emmott.

One of the major announcements involved the historic Middleton Old Grammar School, located on Boarshaw Road. Recently acquired by the council, the school, which dates back to 1582, is expected to announce a new tenant by the end of the year. The council plans to conduct a feasibility study to assess the building's repair and refurbishment, aiming to reopen it for community use in the future. Previously, the site served as a wedding and events venue before being purchased by the council when it became available for sale.

In addition to the school, the council is also in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill and the adjacent London House office block. The aim is to restore Warwick Mill for residential use while demolishing London House. This move is part of a broader strategy to revitalise the area and enhance local housing options.

Furthermore, the Middleton Scout Hut on Long Street, which has been vacant for 13 years, will be transformed into a community venue. The council has secured a long-term lease with the Groundwork Trust, a charitable organisation, to repurpose the building. Plans include creating a hub for workshops focused on ecology and construction skills, as well as providing a space for local environmental projects and activities aimed at young people, thereby addressing social isolation within the community.

articles.title: Businessman Pleads Guilty to Selling £2.4 Million Worth of Fake Clothes in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: A businessman from Hale Barns has pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods with intent to supply after a haul of fake designer clothing worth £2.4 million was discovered in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

16:12, 17 September 2026

Assum Malik from Hale Barns has pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods with intent to supply after a haul of fake designer clothes was discovered in Rochdale.

01:02, 17 September 2026

Assum Malik from Hale Barns has pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods with intent to supply after a significant haul of fake designer clothing was discovered in Rochdale.

23:05, 16 September 2026

A businessman from Hale Barns has pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods with intent to supply after a haul of fake designer clothing worth £2.4 million was discovered in Rochdale.

A businessman from Hale Barns has pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods with intent to supply after a haul of fake designer clothing worth £2.4 million was uncovered at a business in Rochdale on January 28, 2022. Assum Malik, of High Elm Road, initially entered a not guilty plea but changed his plea during a hearing at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court on September 14, 2026.

During the court proceedings, Malik disputed the total value of the counterfeit goods, claiming it was closer to £1.2 million rather than the £2.4 million estimated by Rochdale Council. His defence lawyer, Richard Orme, argued that Malik had purchased a "job lot" of counterfeit stock for £6,000, intending to sell it for around £20,000. However, Judge Jason Macadam stated that the £2.4 million figure represented the potential losses to the legitimate brands had customers purchased the counterfeit items instead.

The court's findings highlight the significant impact of counterfeit goods on legitimate businesses, with the judge emphasising the importance of protecting brand integrity. Malik's case serves as a reminder of the legal consequences associated with the sale of counterfeit merchandise.

As the case progresses, further sentencing details will be determined by the court, and Malik faces potential penalties for his actions. This incident underscores the ongoing issue of counterfeit goods in the retail market, which continues to affect both consumers and legitimate businesses alike.

articles.title: Scout Moor II Wind Farm Plans Reduced Following Community Feedback
articles.excerpt: Developers have scaled back the Scout Moor II wind farm project, reducing the number of proposed turbines from 17 to 12 after consulting with local residents and organisations.
articles.content_html:
Developers have revised plans for the Scout Moor II wind farm, located on moorland between Rochdale and Rossendale, reducing the number of proposed turbines from 17 to 12. This decision follows feedback from local residents and organisations, aiming to address concerns raised during the initial consultation process.

The new wind farm will be situated adjacent to the existing Scout Moor wind farm, with each turbine potentially reaching heights of up to 590 feet (180 metres), making them taller than Blackpool Tower. The revised plans have been submitted to both Rochdale and Rossendale councils for further review and consultation before any approval is granted.

Campaign group Friends of the Moorland has expressed skepticism regarding the revisions, stating that it is unlikely all their concerns will be fully addressed. Steve Davison from the group indicated that a detailed review of the new plans is necessary to form a comprehensive opinion on the changes.

The initial proposals had attracted hundreds of objections, with opponents highlighting potential impacts on peatland, wildlife, and the surrounding landscape. The next steps will involve a further round of consultations, allowing the community to voice their opinions on the updated plans.

articles.title: Ignite Fire Festival Returns to Rochdale from 20 to 22 November 2026
articles.excerpt: The Ignite Fire Festival will return to Rochdale this November, featuring new displays and attractions over three evenings of entertainment, promising to be bigger and better than last year.
articles.content_html:
The Ignite Fire Festival will return to Rochdale from Friday, 20 November to Sunday, 22 November 2026, offering three evenings of free family entertainment. Organisers have promised that this year's festival will be bigger and better than its inaugural event in 2023, featuring new dazzling trails and attractions.

The festival will transform the square and gardens around Rochdale Town Hall, including new pathways and parkland on Broadfield Slopes. Last year, the event attracted over 10,000 attendees, and this year’s programme will include immersive trails of fire, lights, and sound, with displays open to walk through each evening.

Highlights will include fiery displays, blazing sculptures, and an illuminated installation created by the outdoor arts specialists Walk the Plank. The Christmas lights switch-on will also take place on the final evening of the festival, adding to the festive atmosphere.

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, expressed excitement for the event, stating that it will feature performances from local residents trained for the festival, alongside returning acts from Travelling Light Circus. Further details will be announced in October.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The Fairies’ Chapel is part geology and part story — a riverside niche that inspired Victorian storytellers and still sparks local legend, but the stones speak a different language to the folklore.
articles.summary: The Fairies’ Chapel is part geology and part story — a riverside niche that inspired Victorian storytellers and still sparks local legend, but the stones speak a different language to the folklore.
articles.body:
Walk the Spodden through Healey Dell and you’ll come to a narrow cleft the locals call the Thrutch, where the water has hollowed a church‑like niche in the rock. The name “Fairies’ Chapel” belongs to that place: it’s a charming local toponym and a focus for the Dell’s long tradition of storytelling — but the site itself is a recognised nature reserve with a heritage centre, visitor facilities and an industrial‑archaeological story that you can confirm on the borough’s website. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The Dell’s human record is plain: the valley hosts mill ruins, lodges, a recreated heritage centre and a former Lancashire & Yorkshire Railway viaduct now recorded on the National Heritage List for England (Healey Dell Viaduct, Grade II). Those are facts you can check in official listings and conservation records; the viaduct’s listed status is part of the site’s documented history rather than its fairy lore. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

The fairies arrive in the written record through collectors of local tradition. The best‑known literary source is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (first published 1829), which prints a full romance of the Fairies’ Chapel: a miller, a Lady Eleanor, a Fairy Queen and prophecies tied to a grotto beyond the waterfall. Roby’s work is an important record of regional storytelling, but it is a collection of folklore and narrative rather than an archival record of events. In other words, Roby preserves what people told one another; he does not provide independent proof that supernatural beings lived in the Dell. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

Local interpretive material — including the Healey Dell Heritage Centre — explains how geology and water action could produce the “pulpit, reading desk and seats” that earlier visitors described, and it records that part of the feature described as the chapel was lost in a great flood in the 1830s. The precise year reported varies between accounts: the heritage guide names a flood on 4 July 1838, while other long‑running guides give 1839 as the date. That discrepancy shows how oral and popular histories can diverge from contemporary documentary records; I could not find a single primary archive entry here that settles which year is definitively correct. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/history/))

So: are there really fairies in Healey Dell? If you mean literal supernatural beings, there is no verifiable documentary evidence to support their existence — references are folklore, literary retelling and local tradition rather than legal records, surveys or conservation reports. If you mean has the place inspired and preserved stories of fairies, witches and a Fairy King, the answer is an emphatic yes: those tales have been collected, retold and used to interpret the landscape for well over a century, and they form an important part of local cultural heritage. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

Visitors today can enjoy both layers: the real, recorded features of the Dell (wildlife, waterfalls, mill remains and a listed viaduct) and the imaginative pleasures of a place that has gathered romance and regional folklore. Treat the Fairies’ Chapel as you would any good local story — a memorable part of Healey’s identity that sits alongside verifiable history, not in its place.

In 1871 The Black Dyke Band performed at the original opening ceremony for Rochdale Town Hall. Since the post refurbishment of the Town Hall, the band have since gone on to perform every year bringing the best of brass band quality for all to enjoy. Join them again in 2027.
